samples.summary: Gate 1's "newest CI run wins" rule — which this delta's new test now pins as the contract — has no deterministic tie-break and is not fail-closed, so a red CI run for the head SHA can be masked by a same-timestamp green one
samples.evidence: `ciPassed` reduces all CI evidence for the head SHA to `runs[0].conclusion === "success"` after `runs.sort((a, b) => new Date(b.created_at ?? 0) - new Date(a.created_at ?? 0))` (mark-ready.mjs:136-137). `created_at` from the Actions API is ISO-8601 at SECOND granularity, so two distinct CI runs for the same head SHA created in the same second compare equal, the comparator returns 0, and the survivor is whatever order the API page happened to be in — not "the newest". The comparator is also NaN for an unparseable `created_at` (only `null`/`undefined` are coerced by `?? 0`), which again degrades to page order. The new test (mark-ready.test.mjs:236-246) explicitly blesses the shape an attacker needs — "a red CI run for this SHA exists, and gate 1 still promotes because another run is greener" — while asserting nothing about the ambiguous case. A fail-closed formulation (every `CI` run for the SHA must be `success`, or tie-break on `id`/`run_number` descending) removes the ambiguity without weakening the legitimate re-run case. Exploitability is limited today because the promote job additionally requires `needs.ci.outputs.conclusion == 'success'` for the triggering run (agent-review-panel.yml:1455), which is why confidence is low — but mark-ready is also invoked as a standalone gate and its own header claims gate 1 is authoritative.

samples.summary: Gate 1 identifies its "unforgeable" CI evidence by the workflow's mutable DISPLAY NAME rather than by workflow path/id — the exact surface the doc in this delta names as the forgery vector
samples.evidence: `(data.workflow_runs ?? []).filter((r) => r.name === "CI")` (mark-ready.mjs:133) matches on the run's display name. The delta's own threat model says so out loud: "an agent branch can add a `push`-triggered workflow named `CI` that concludes `success` on its own head SHA (gate 1, which matches on the run's display name)" (docs/tasks/active/20260825-promote-exit-code-default-todo.md:97-99). The only thing standing between that and a satisfied gate 1 is an installation permission held outside the repo (`workflows`), i.e. a control this repository cannot assert or test. Matching the run's `path === ".github/workflows/ci.yml"` (or its `workflow_id`) instead would tie gate 1 to a specific, branch-protected file and make the gate defensible on its own rather than solely on the absence of a GitHub App scope. I verified no other workflow in `.github/workflows/` currently uses `name: CI`, so this is defense-in-depth today, not a live bypass.
searchedFor: Grep '^name:' across .github/workflows (only ci.yml is named CI)

samples.summary: The delta's expanded trust model restates gate 1 as UNFORGEABLE without noting that the CI run's CONCLUSION is produced by executing the PR branch's own code, so a branch that neuters its own lanes yields a genuinely green run
samples.evidence: The new section asserts "`mark-ready.mjs`'s header calls gates 1 and 2 UNFORGEABLE because 'the author agent cannot create or forge a CI run'" (todo.md:93-95) and treats the missing `workflows` scope as the whole of gate 1's integrity. But `ci.yml` runs the branch's own tree: the `changes` job executes `node ./scripts/changed-areas.mjs` from the PR checkout (ci.yml:149) and `verify-self` runs `pnpm verify:self` — ci.yml:30-35 itself calls that "arbitrary build and test code from the pull request's own tree". An agent branch that edits its own lane scripts, `harness.config.json`, or a test file gets a real CI run, named CI, that concludes `success`; gate 1 then reads green and mark-ready posts a hand-off comment telling the human reviewer "✅ CI verification (`verify:self` and `verify:integration`) is green" (mark-ready.mjs:249). Unforgeability holds for the run's EXISTENCE and identity, not for what it verified, and the doc that is now the trust model of record should say which of the two it means so the next reader does not treat gate 1 as content integrity.

samples.summary: The newly-documented invariant "the App must NOT hold Workflows: write, and no other workflow may be named CI" is enforced by nothing mechanical
samples.evidence: This delta promotes "the App must NOT be granted `Workflows: write`" from a follow-up suggestion to the load-bearing part of the loop's trust model (todo.md:84-101), and gate 1's `r.name === "CI"` filter plus gate 2's checks:write assumption both rest on it. Nothing in the repo asserts either half: there is no test that fails if a second workflow is added with `name: CI`, none that fails if a job outside the `workflow_run`-triggered panel gains `checks: write`, and the permission itself lives on the GitHub App installation where no lane can see it. The consequence is that a future PR can silently dissolve the invariant this doc just declared, and the only record will be prose. A cheap mechanical guard (assert exactly one workflow file with `name: CI`, and that `checks: write` appears only in `agent-review-panel.yml`) would make the trust model testable; I could not find one.
searchedFor: Grep 'workflows: write|Workflows: write|workflows permission|name: CI' repo-wide (hits only docs, mark-ready.mjs, ci*.yml)

verdict.reason: The cited code exists (mark-ready.mjs:133-137 sorts CI runs by created_at desc and reads only runs[0].conclusion), but it is not a blocking security defect under the security rubric. (a) The ambiguous tie is only reachable when a green CI run for the head SHA already exists, in which case the deterministic newest-wins rule already permits promotion — the missing tie-break confers no capability an attacker lacks. (b) An attacker cannot mint a divergent second CI run for the same head SHA: ci.yml triggers only on push-to-main, pull_request-to-main and merge_group (whose head_sha is the speculative merge commit); there is no workflow_dispatch, and two pull_request runs for the same commit execute the identical tree, so divergence needs flakiness, not attacker control. (c) The only automated --promote call site (agent-review-panel.yml:1499, the sole hit across all workflows) is additionally gated by needs.ci.outputs.conclusion == 'success' (agent-review-panel.yml:1454-1456) on the triggering run; the other reference (spec-to-pr.mjs:268) is a dry-run hint with no --promote. (d) Impact ceiling is a draft→ready flip plus label/comment — mark-ready never merges (mark-ready.mjs:22-25) and merging red code is independently blocked by classic branch protection's required verify-* contexts (MAINTAINING.md:202-217). (e) The NaN comparator path needs a malformed created_at from the Actions API, which no actor in this threat model controls. The residual issue is nondeterminism/robustness — already captured by the correctness lens (.agent-review/correctness/summary.md:5) — i.e. at most a minor hardening suggestion (tie-break on id/run_number), not a major security weakness.

finding.summary: New task doc recommends granting the agent GitHub App `Workflows: write`, which would defeat both "unforgeable" ready gates
finding.evidence: The doc added by this change states: "**The follow-up that matters is the permission itself** — grant the App `Workflows: write`" (todo line 83). The panel's own trust model depends on the opposite: `.github/workflows/agent-review-panel.yml:46-52` says the `workflow_run` trigger "is a SECURITY boundary" precisely because "The agent App cannot push `.github/workflows/**`", and mark-ready.mjs:1-14 claims gates 1 and 2 are "UNFORGEABLE" because "the author agent cannot create or forge a CI run" and "Only the reviewer workflow (which has checks:write) can post that check". Both claims are consequences of the App lacking workflow-write. Grant it, and an agent-authored `agent/*` branch can add (a) a workflow file whose `name:` is `CI`, triggered on `push`, producing a run named "CI" with conclusion `success` for its own head SHA — which is exactly what `ciPassed` reads (scripts/agent/mark-ready.mjs:133) — and (b) a push-triggered workflow with `permissions: checks: write` that posts `agent-review-<lens>` check runs with conclusion `success` on the same SHA, satisfying gate 2 via `allRequiredPassed`. Both gates then read as green with zero independent evidence and the promote job flips the PR to ready with the App token. The doc presents the grant as the preferred follow-up with no mention of this consequence; the alternative it offers second (an explicit "the agent does not edit workflow files" policy) is the one that preserves the boundary.

verdict.reason: The quoted recommendation does not exist in the repository; the doc states the opposite. A repo-wide grep for "Workflows: write" finds exactly one occurrence in source, at docs/tasks/active/20260825-promote-exit-code-default-todo.md:84, and it reads: "**The App must NOT be granted `Workflows: write` to fix this.** That was this doc's first recommendation and it is wrong: the missing permission is not an oversight, it is the load-bearing part of the loop's trust model." Lines 87-101 then lay out the exact forgery chain the finding describes (a push-triggered workflow named `CI` satisfying gate 1, and one with `checks: write` posting its own `agent-review-*` runs for gate 2) as the justification for NOT granting it, citing agent-review-panel.yml's `workflow_run` rationale and mark-ready.mjs's UNFORGEABLE header. Lines 103-106 give the boundary-preserving policy ("the agent does not edit workflow files") as the sole recommended follow-up, not as a second-place alternative. The companion lessons file at 20260825-promote-exit-code-default-lessons.md:37-46 records the same reversal explicitly ("this task's first draft recommended granting it. It is the reverse… Before proposing to widen a permission, grep for what currently depends on its absence"). The only other matches for the phrase are .agent-review/docs/summary.md:3 and verdict.json:3, which are this finding's own review-output artifacts, not repository source. The finding was evidently written against a superseded draft; the working-tree doc is a warning against the grant, containing the identical threat model. Secondarily, a markdown doc grants no permission, so even a real recommendation would not itself be an exploitable weakening of the enforced path.

finding.summary: Gate 1's "unforgeable" CI evidence is matched by workflow DISPLAY NAME, not workflow path/id — a branch-added workflow named `CI` forges it, and this change pins the name filter as the invariant
finding.evidence: `ciPassed` selects evidence with `(data.workflow_runs ?? []).filter((r) => r.name === "CI")` and then takes the newest by `created_at` (mark-ready.mjs:133-137). `name` is the run's display name, which is whatever the workflow file's `name:` key says — it is not tied to `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Anyone who can push a branch to the BASE repo can add `.github/workflows/anything.yml` with `name: CI` on `push`; its run is recorded against the same `head_sha`, is newer than the real CI run, and `runs[0].conclusion === "success"` returns true even when the genuine CI run for that SHA failed. That path is not hypothetical for this repo: the panel's own header notes "The agent App cannot push `.github/workflows/**`, but an `agent:managed` human PR can" (.github/workflows/agent-review-panel.yml:51), and `agent:managed` is an opt-in label (line 190) that puts such a PR on the promote path. The new test added here (`scripts/agent/mark-ready.test.mjs:184-209`) elevates this name filter to a pinned security property while only exercising differently-NAMED runs, so it documents the check as sound rather than exposing the same-name forge. `set-state.mjs:226` filters CI the same way. A robust filter would key on `r.path === ".github/workflows/ci.yml"` (or `workflow_id`), which cannot be spoofed by a second file.

verdict.reason: Code is present exactly as claimed: mark-ready.mjs:133-137 keys gate 1's "unforgeable CI evidence" on the run's DISPLAY name (`r.name === "CI"`), sorts newest-first, and reads only `runs[0].conclusion`. `name` comes from a workflow file's `name:` key, not from `path`/`workflow_id`, so it is not bound to .github/workflows/ci.yml (grep confirms ci.yml:4 is the only current `name: CI`). A second workflow file on the head branch with `name: CI` on `push` yields a run against the same head_sha, newer than the genuine one, and satisfies the gate even when real CI failed — contradicting the module header's claim at mark-ready.mjs:4-10 that the run cannot be forged. Reachability is documented by the repo itself: agent-review-panel.yml:46-52 states the agent App cannot push `.github/workflows/**` "but an `agent:managed` human PR can", and such a PR reaches promote (agent-review-panel.yml:1444-1456, 1499), whose only CI condition is `needs.ci.outputs.conclusion == 'success'` derived from a trigger that is itself name-keyed (`workflows: ["CI"]`, line 28). No guard re-derives the workflow path/id anywhere on that path, so `already-guarded` does not apply; the App's missing workflows:write blocks only the agent, not the agent:managed human path the panel header names. The new test (mark-ready.test.mjs:184-209) pins the name filter as a security property while exercising only differently-named runs, and mark-ready.test.mjs:211-231 pins newest-wins, which is what lets the forged newer run outrank a red genuine one. set-state.mjs:226 repeats the same filter. In lane (weakened integrity check on an authorization/evidence gate) and blocking at major.
